title: Primariness of the spaces \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) for \(1\leq p\leq\infty\)
author: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: We prove that the spaces \(\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\) and \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) have the uniform primary factorisation property whenever \(\alpha\) is an ordinal and \(1<p\leq\infty\). For the case \(p=1\), we establish a general criterion ensuring that \(\ell_{1}(X)\) inherits the uniform primary factorisation property from \(X\). As a consequence, \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) is primary for every compact metrizable space \(K\) and every \(1\leq p\leq\infty\).

Introduction and organisation

−

A Banach space \(X\) is said to be primary if it cannot be decomposed, in a complemented sense, into two essentially different pieces. More precisely, \(X\) is primary if, whenever \(P\colon X\to X\) is a projection, either \(PX\) or \((I_{X}-P)X\) is isomorphic to \(X\).

The primariness problem for the classical Banach spaces played an important role in the development of the isomorphic theory of Banach spaces during the 1960s and 1970s. The first major successes concerned the sequence spaces: Pełczyński proved the stronger property of primeness for \(c_{0}\) and \(\ell_{p}\), \(1\leq p<\infty\) , and Lindenstrauss obtained the corresponding result for \(\ell_{\infty}\) . This was followed by the primariness of \(C[0,1]\), proved by Lindenstrauss and Pełczyński , and of \(L_{p}\), \(1\leq p<\infty\), obtained from Enflo’s ideas as presented by Maurey . The spaces \(C(\alpha)\) of continuous functions on ordinal intervals were then treated by Billard in the countable case and by Alspach and Benyamini in full generality . Taken together, these results provided a positive solution to the primariness problem for classical spaces and introduced powerful methods for analysing their geometry.

The primariness of many other Banach spaces has also been established over the years; we refer the reader to for a more detailed account. A particularly important direction concerns bi-parameter spaces, that is, spaces obtained by combining two classical Banach spaces. In the sequence-space setting, the corresponding results for the spaces \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{q})\), \(1\leq p,q\leq\infty\), were obtained through the work of Casazza–Kottman–Lin and Capon . These results naturally extend to multi-parameter sequence spaces; see the paper of the present author and Kania .

Bi-parameter spaces involving \(L_{p}\)-spaces form another major part of this picture. In that direction, Capon developed a substantial analysis of mixed \(L_{p}\)-spaces, establishing the primariness of the spaces \(L_{r}(L_{s})\), \(\ell_{p}(L_{q})\) and \(L_{p}(\ell_{q})\) for \(1<r,s<\infty\) and \(1\leq p,q<\infty\) . The corresponding \(\ell_{\infty}\)-sums required separate methods: Wark proved the primariness of \(\ell_{\infty}(L_{p})\) for \(1<p<\infty\) , and Müller subsequently treated \(\ell_{\infty}(L_{1})\) . More recently, Lechner, Motakis, Müller and Schlumprecht proved the primariness of \(L_{1}(L_{p})\), \(1<p<\infty\) , and pointed out several remaining unresolved primariness problems for classical bi-parameter spaces.

Motivated by this broader programme, this paper studies bi-parameter spaces involving \(C(K)\)-spaces, a class for which the corresponding primariness problems have so far remained largely open. More precisely, we study \(\ell_{p}\)-sums of \(C(K)\)-spaces. Previously known primariness results for spaces of the form \(\ell_{p}(X)\) typically relied on properties of a basis of \(X\), perhaps with \(\ell_{p}(L_{1})\) being a notable exception. Such methods do not appear to be directly applicable in the \(C(K)\)-space setting. The approach taken here is instead based on the reproducibility properties of \(C(K)\) itself, together with the structure of the underlying compact space \(K\). This naturally brings the primary factorisation property into play. Recall that the (uniform) primary factorisation property, denoted by (U)PFP, asserts a dichotomy for operators on the space in terms of factorisation of the identity; see Definition 2.2 for details. The same point of view was used by the present author and Kania in the context of primariness of uncountable \(\ell_{p}\)-sums; see .

Our main results are as follows.

For every ordinal \(\alpha\) and every \(1<p\leq\infty\), the space \(\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\) has the UPFP. In particular, these spaces are primary.

Using similar methods, we also obtain the corresponding result for the uncountable compact metric case.

For every \(1<p\leq\infty\), the space \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) has the UPFP. In particular, these spaces are primary.

Finally, we treat the case \(p=1\); in this case, we obtain a general criterion ensuring that the UPFP is transferred to the corresponding \(\ell_{1}\)-sum.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space such that either \(X\simeq c_{0}(X)\) or \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1<p\leq\infty\). Suppose moreover that \(X\) contains no complemented copy of \(\ell_{1}\). Then the UPFP passes from \(X\) to \(\ell_{1}(X)\); that is, if \(X\) has the UPFP, then \(\ell_{1}(X)\) has the UPFP. In particular, \(\ell_{1}(X)\) is primary.

Combining these results with Milutin’s theorem and the Bessaga–Pełczyński classification of the spaces \(C(K)\) for countable compact metric spaces , we obtain a complete answer to one of the problems listed in , which motivated our interest in this question.

Let \(K\) be a compact metric space and let \(1\leq p\leq\infty\). Then \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) is primary.

The proofs of these theorems rely on reducing operators \(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K))\) to diagonal form. This is achieved in two steps: by reducing to upper triangular operators, and by reducing to lower triangular operators. Together, these reductions yield the desired diagonal form. At that point, one can factorise the identity by invoking the UPFP of the underlying space \(C(K)\).

Lastly, although our original motivation was to treat the case \(C(K)\) where \(K\) is metrizable, the methods developed here are not inherently limited to that setting. They appear to apply more broadly to other sums of the form \(\ell_{p}(X)\), where \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), especially when \(X\) is a \(C(K)\)-space. For example, the same reductions to diagonal operators apply when \(K\) is the double arrow space \(K_{\mathrm{d.a.}}\). Thus, provided one can argue that \(C(K_{\mathrm{d.a.}})\) has the UPFP, it would follow that \(\ell_{p}(C(K_{\mathrm{d.a.}}))\) has the UPFP, and hence is primary, for every \(1\leq p\leq\infty\). This may already be implicit in Michalak’s proof of the primariness of \(C(K_{\mathrm{d.a.}})\) , but we have not checked the required uniform estimates.

Organisation.

−

We briefly describe the structure of the paper. In Section 2 we introduce the notation used throughout, and recall some background results concerning the topology of the ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) and the unit interval \([0,1]\), as well as operators on \(C(\alpha)\) and \(C[0,1]\). The main technical work is carried out in Sections 3, 4 and 5. In Section 3 we prove the upper and lower triangular reductions for the spaces \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\), \(1<p<\infty\), while in Section 4 we treat the case \(p=1\). The corresponding arguments for \(\ell_{\infty}\)-sums, where one must take additional care with operator matrices, are given in Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, we use these technical reductions to prove Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3.

2.

Notation and preliminary results

−
2.1.

Definitions and basic notation

−

We follow standard notation and conventions unless stated otherwise. Throughout, the scalar field, denoted by \(\mathbb{K}\), may be either \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\). We reserve the term operator for bounded linear maps between Banach spaces; thus, operators are always assumed to be bounded. For a Banach space \(X\), we write \(I_{X}\colon X\to X\) for the identity operator on \(X\), \(B_{X}\) for its unit ball and \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) for the space of operators on \(X\). More specialized notation will be introduced as needed.

Let \(T\colon X\to Y\) and \(S\colon Z\to W\) be operators between Banach spaces \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) and \(W\). We say that \(S\) factors through \(T\) with constant \(C\) if there exist operators \(V\colon Z\to X\) and \(U\colon Y\to W\) such that

\(UTV=S\quad\text{and}\quad\|U\|\|V\|\leq C.\)

If this holds for some constant \(C\geq 1\), then we simply say that \(S\) factors through \(T\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space.

  1. (a)

    We say that \(X\) has the primary factorisation property (PFP) if for every bounded operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(C\geq 1\). We say that \(X\) has the \(C\)-primary factorisation property (\(C\)-PFP) if, for every operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\) with constant \(C\).

  3. (c)

    We say that \(X\) has the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP) if there exists \(C\geq 1\) such that \(X\) has the \(C\)-PFP.

2.1.1.

Sums of Banach spaces with respect to an unconditional basis.

−

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \((X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence of Banach spaces. We define the \(E\)-direct sum of these spaces by

\(\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X_{n}\right)_{E}=\left\{x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X_{n}:\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|x_{n}\|e_{n}\in E\right\},\)

and equip it with the norm

\(\|(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|=\left\|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|x_{n}\|e_{n}\right\|,\)

which makes it a Banach space. In the case where all the spaces \(X_{n}\) are equal to a space \(X\), we simply denote this space by \(E(\mathbb{N},X)\). In the particular case of \(\ell_{p}\)-spaces, we mostly omit the index set \(\mathbb{N}\) and write \(\ell_{p}(X)\) for \(\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},X)\). Observe that this sum depends not only on the Banach space \(E\), but also on the choice of basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\); however, this dependence will remain implicit throughout.

We consider now the case where \(X_{n}=X\) for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). For each \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in E(\mathbb{N},X)\), we define the support of \(x\) by

\(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:x_{n}\neq 0\}.\)

For each \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we define the closed subspace

\(E(M,X)=\{x\in E(\mathbb{N},X):\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq M\}\subseteq E(\mathbb{N},X),\)

and let \(P_{M}\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(M,X)\) and \(J_{M}\colon E(M,X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X)\) denote the canonical projection and inclusion, respectively. Then, naturally, \(P_{M}J_{M}=I_{E(M,X)}\). In the case where \(M=\{m\}\) is a singleton, we simply write \(P_{m}\) and \(J_{m}\) in place of \(P_{\{m\}}\) and \(J_{\{m\}}\).

To each operator \(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X)\) we can associate a matrix of operators \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\) in the natural way, namely by defining \(T_{n,m}\colon X\to X\) by

\(T_{n,m}=P_{n}TJ_{m}.\)

Then, for all \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) and all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we have

\(P_{n}Tx=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}T_{n,m}x_{m}.\)

Let \(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X)\) be an operator with matrix representation \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). We say that \(T\) is upper triangular if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n>m.\)

Similarly, we say that \(T\) is lower triangular if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n<m.\)

If \(T\) is both upper and lower triangular, we say that \(T\) is diagonal.

Let \((T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence of operators \(T_{n}\colon X\to X\) such that \(\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_{n}\|<\infty\). Then we may define the diagonal operator

\(T=\operatorname{diag}(T_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N})\)

to be the operator \(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X)\) given by

\(P_{m}Tx=T_{m}x_{m}\)

for all \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). It is clear that \(T\) is an operator and that

\(\|T\|=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_{n}\|.\)
2.1.2.

The \(\ell_{\infty}\) case.

−

For a sequence \((X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) of Banach spaces, one analogously defines the \(\ell_{\infty}\)-direct sum

\(\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X_{n}\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}=\left\{x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X_{n}:\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|x_{n}\|<\infty\right\},\)

equipped with the norm

\(\|(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|x_{n}\|.\)

In the case where \(X_{n}=X\) for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we simply write \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\). We carry over most of the notation introduced above in the natural way. Thus, for instance, if \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we still write \(\ell_{\infty}(M,X)\) for the closed subspace consisting of those elements whose support is contained in \(M\), and we denote by \(P_{M}\) and \(J_{M}\) the canonical projection and inclusion, respectively.

Moreover, for an operator \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\), we may still associate to it an operator matrix \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\) by setting

\(T_{n,m}=P_{n}TJ_{m}.\)

However, in this setting, one must proceed with care, since the matrix does not, in general, determine the operator, as the following elementary example shows.

Let \(X=\mathbb{K}\) and consider the operator \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(\mathbb{K})\to\ell_{\infty}(\mathbb{K})\) given by

\(Tx=(\Lambda(x),0,0,\dots),\)

where \(\Lambda\) is a Banach limit; see, for instance, . Thus \(\Lambda\in\ell_{\infty}^{*}\), and \(\Lambda\) agrees with the usual limit on convergent sequences. In particular, \(\Lambda\) vanishes on \(c_{0}\). Hence \(T\neq 0\), while \(T_{n,m}=P_{n}TJ_{m}=0\) for all \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\), since \(J_{m}\mathbb{K}\subseteq c_{0}\).

Thus, in contrast with the case of unconditional sums, the operator matrix does not in general suffice to describe the behaviour of an operator. This leads us to introduce the following stronger notion of lower triangularity.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator. We say that \(T\) is lower triangular if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n<m,\)

and, moreover, \(T\) acts according to its matrix, in the sense that

\(P_{n}Tx=\sum_{m\leq n}T_{n,m}x_{m}\)

for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\).

Similarly, we strengthen the notion of a diagonal operator.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator. We say that \(T\) is diagonal if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n\neq m,\)

and, moreover, \(T\) acts according to its matrix, in the sense that

\(P_{m}Tx=T_{m,m}x_{m}\)

for all \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\).

Naturally, given a uniformly bounded sequence of operators \(T_{n}:X\to X\), we can still define the associated diagonal operator \(T=\operatorname{diag}(T_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N})\).

2.2.

Background and topological results in \(C(\alpha)\)

−

We recall some standard topological notions, following the notation and presentation of Alspach and Benyamini . If \(A\) is a subset of a topological space, we write \(A^{(1)}\) for the set of accumulation points of \(A\). The higher derived sets are then defined recursively by setting \(A^{(\alpha+1)}=\bigl(A^{(\alpha)}\bigr)^{(1)}\) for each ordinal \(\alpha\), and \(A^{(\alpha)}=\bigcap_{\beta<\alpha}A^{(\beta)}\) whenever \(\alpha\) is a limit ordinal. If, for some ordinal \(\alpha\), the set \(A^{(\alpha)}\) is finite of cardinality \(n\), then \((\alpha,n)\) is called the characteristic system of \(A\).

Now let \(A\) be a compact subset of an ordinal space. In this case, the subspace topology on \(A\) coincides with the order topology inherited by \(A\). Consequently, there is an ordinal \(\alpha\) such that \(A^{(\alpha)}\) is finite. We denote this \(\alpha\) by \(\tau(A)\) and refer to it as the type of \(A\). Moreover, two compact subsets of ordinal spaces are homeomorphic if and only if they have the same characteristic system; see, for instance, . In particular, we shall use the following classical consequence.

For the interval formula below, assume η > 0. If η = 0, A is instead a finite discrete set of n points.

Let \(A\) be a compact subset of an ordinal space with characteristic system \((\eta,n)\), where \(\eta\) is an ordinal and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Then \(A\) is homeomorphic to \([0,\omega^{\eta}\cdot n]\).

Correction in this reading edition

The ordinal interval formula applies to positive Cantor–Bendixson rank. At rank zero, A is a finite discrete set of n points, while [0, n] has n + 1 points. The finite case is stated separately here.

We also record the following elementary fact.

(Finite indivisibility of closed subsets of ordinal intervals).

Let \(A\) be a closed subset of an ordinal space with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\) for some ordinal \(\eta\). Suppose that \(A_{1},\dots,A_{N}\subseteq A\) are closed subsets such that \(A=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}\). Then there exists \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(A_{n_{0}}\) is homeomorphic to \(A\).

Proof.Fold proof

Since \(A\) has characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), the set \(A^{(\eta)}\) consists of exactly one point, say \(A^{(\eta)}=\{a\}\). Since derived sets commute with finite unions of closed sets, we have

\(\{a\}=A^{(\eta)}=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}^{(\eta)}.\)

It follows that there exists \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(A_{n_{0}}^{(\eta)}=\{a\}\). Therefore, \(A_{n_{0}}\) has characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and hence \(A_{n_{0}}\) is homeomorphic to \(A\) by Theorem 2.6. ∎

We will need the following definition.

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space and let \(A\subseteq K\) be closed. Denote by \(R_{A}\colon C(K)\to C(A)\) the restriction operator. We say that an operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C(K)\) is a simultaneous extension operator if

\(R_{A}S_{A}=I_{C(A)}.\)

We now introduce several facts concerning operators acting on \(C(\alpha)\), as proven by Alspach and Benyamini. We start with the existence of a simultaneous extension operator .

(Simultaneous extension operator).

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal, and let \(A\) be a closed subset of \([0,\alpha]\). Then there exists a norm-one simultaneous extension operator

\(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C(\alpha).\)

We shall also need the following consequence of the main result of Alspach and Benyamini .

(Alspach–Benyamini).

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Suppose that \(C(\alpha)\) is not isomorphic to \(C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular ordinal \(\xi\) and any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq 2\). Then \(C(\alpha)\) has the UPFP.

The previous theorem is not stated explicitly in this form in , but it can be extracted directly from the proof of their main result; see for a detailed exposition. Moreover, the estimates in each step can be made quantitative. Since the UPFP is preserved under isomorphisms , this yields the stated UPFP conclusion for the ordinal spaces covered by Theorem 2.10.

2.3.

Background and topological results in \(C[0,1]\)

−

Similarly, we recall some background results for the unit interval \([0,1]\). We have the following formulation for topological indivisibility in this case.

(Countable topological indivisibility of \([0,1]\)).

Let \((A_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of closed subsets of \([0,1]\) such that

\([0,1]=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_{n}.\)

Then there exist \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) and a closed subset \(A\subseteq A_{n_{0}}\) such that \(A\) is homeomorphic to \([0,1]\).

Proof.Fold proof

Since \([0,1]\) is compact and metrizable, it is a Baire space. Hence, it cannot be written as a countable union of closed subsets with empty interior. Therefore there exists \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(A_{n_{0}}\) has non-empty interior in \([0,1]\).

Choose a non-empty relatively open subset \(U\) of \([0,1]\) such that \(U\subseteq A_{n_{0}}\). Since \(U\) is non-empty and relatively open in \([0,1]\), it contains a non-degenerate closed interval \(A=[a,b]\), with \(a<b\). Then \(A\) is homeomorphic to \([0,1]\), and \(A\subseteq A_{n_{0}}\). ∎

We also record the following special case of the Borsuk–Dugundji extension theorem, see , which is the only form needed in what follows.

(Borsuk–Dugundji extension theorem).

Assume that A is nonempty.

Let \(A\) be a closed subset of \([0,1]\). Then there exists a norm-one simultaneous extension operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C[0,1]\).

Correction in this reading edition

The norm-one conclusion requires A to be nonempty. For A empty, its function space is zero and the extension has norm zero.

Throughout this paper, \(A\) will be a closed interval, so one does not need the full strength of the Borsuk–Dugundji extension theorem. Indeed, if \(A=[a,b]\subseteq[0,1]\), a norm-one extension operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C[0,1]\) can be obtained by linear interpolation.

Finally, we record that \(C[0,1]\) has the UPFP. The quantitative form needed for the UPFP can be extracted from Weis’ proof of a theorem of Rosenthal . The same conclusion may already be implicit in Rosenthal’s original argument, although we have not verified this.

The space \(C[0,1]\) has the UPFP.

Proof.Fold proof

For an operator \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C[0,1])\), denote by \(\omega_{T}(t)\) the oscillation of the representing kernel \((T^{*}\delta_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}\), as in . We shall use that the oscillation is subadditive: if \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(C[0,1])\), then

\(\omega_{T+S}(t)\leq\omega_{T}(t)+\omega_{S}(t)\)

for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Thus, fixing an operator \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C[0,1])\), we show that it satisfies the dichotomy for the UPFP.

Since the representing kernel of \(I_{C[0,1]}\) is \(t\mapsto\delta_{t}\), and since \(\|\delta_{s}-\delta_{t}\|=2\) whenever \(s\neq t\), we have \(\omega_{I_{C[0,1]}}(t)=2\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Hence

\(2=\omega_{I_{C[0,1]}}(t)\leq\omega_{T}(t)+\omega_{I_{C[0,1]}-T}(t)\)

for every \(t\in[0,1]\). The sets

\(A=\{t\in[0,1]:\omega_{T}(t)\geq 1\},\qquad B=\{t\in[0,1]:\omega_{I_{C[0,1]}-T}(t)\geq 1\}\)

are closed since \(\omega_{T}\) and \(\omega_{I_{C[0,1]}-T}\) are upper semi-continuous, and they cover \([0,1]\) by the previous inequality. By the Baire category theorem, one of them has non-empty interior. Suppose first that \(A\) has non-empty interior. Since \(\omega_{T}\) is an upper semi-continuous function, the set of its continuity points is a dense \(G_{\delta}\)-set, so that we may choose \(t_{0}\in\operatorname{int}(A)\) at which \(\omega_{T}\) is continuous. This implies, in particular, that \(\omega_{T}(t_{0})\geq 1\).

We now follow the proof of . Denote by \(\Delta\) the Cantor set. The estimates in that proof are quantitative: if \(\omega_{T}(t_{0})\) is bounded below at a point of continuity of \(\omega_{T}\), then the identity on \(C(\Delta)\) factors through \(T\) with a constant depending only on this lower bound. Applying this and using \(\omega_{T}(t_{0})\geq 1\), we obtain operators \(U\) and \(V\) such that

\(UTV=I_{C(\Delta)}\)

and \(\|U\|\|V\|\leq C\), where \(C\) is independent of \(T\).

We observe that, although Weis writes the proof for the real scalar field, the same argument applies over the complex scalar field. The measure-theoretic part uses only the Lebesgue decomposition of finite Radon measures, total variation and mutual singularity. At the point where positive and negative parts of signed measures are used, one instead applies the Jordan decomposition to the real and imaginary parts of the relevant complex measures. This changes, at most, the absolute constant.

Since \(C(\Delta)\) is isomorphic to \(C[0,1]\), it follows that \(I_{C[0,1]}\) factors through \(T\) with constant bounded independently of \(T\). If instead \(B\) has non-empty interior, the same argument applied to \(I_{C[0,1]}-T\) gives the corresponding factorisation through \(I_{C[0,1]}-T\). Therefore, \(C[0,1]\) has the UPFP. ∎

3.

Results for matrix operators

−
3.1.

Reduction to upper triangular form.

−
3.1.1.

The \(C(\alpha)\) case

−

We begin by proving that, under suitable structural assumptions, one may pass to a subcopy of the basis on which the operator \(T\) has upper triangular form. Since this argument works, without additional work, in a fairly general setting, we state the result at that level of generality. The underlying ideas are essentially those already present in , where the interplay between operators \(S\colon X\to E\) and operators on the \(E\)-unconditional sum of \(X\) is studied. Before stating the result, we require the following lemma.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon X\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\)

we have

\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\|T_{n}\|=0.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that the conclusion fails. Then there exist an operator

\(T\colon X\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), there exists \(n>N\) with \(\|T_{n}\|\geq\varepsilon\).

Hence, we may choose a strictly increasing sequence \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|T_{n_{k}}\|\geq\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }k\in\mathbb{N}.\)

For each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), choose \(x_{k}\in B_{X}\) such that \(\|T_{n_{k}}x_{k}\|>\varepsilon/2\). By the Hahn–Banach theorem, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) there exists \(x_{k}^{*}\in B_{X^{*}}\) such that \(x_{k}^{*}(T_{n_{k}}x_{k})>\varepsilon/2.\)

Define an operator \(D\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E\) by

\(D\bigl((x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\bigr)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{k}^{*}(x_{n_{k}})e_{n_{k}},\qquad(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in E(\mathbb{N},X).\)

Since the basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is \(1\)-unconditional and \(\|x_{k}^{*}\|\leq 1\) for all \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), it follows that \(D\) is a bounded linear operator. Set \(\widehat{T}=D\circ T\colon X\to E\). By assumption, the operator \(\widehat{T}\) is compact, so the sequence \((\widehat{T}x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) has a norm-convergent subsequence. Passing to a subsequence, we may suppose that \((\widehat{T}x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) converges in norm to some \(y\in E\).

For each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), from the construction we have

\(e_{n_{k}}^{*}(\widehat{T}x_{k})=x_{k}^{*}(T_{n_{k}}x_{k})>\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.\)

Since \(\|e_{n_{k}}^{*}\|=1\) for all \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), it follows that

\(\bigl|e_{n_{k}}^{*}(y)\bigr|\geq\bigl|e_{n_{k}}^{*}(\widehat{T}x_{k})\bigr|-\|\widehat{T}x_{k}-y\|>\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-\|\widehat{T}x_{k}-y\|.\)

Since \(\widehat{T}x_{k}\to y\) in norm, it follows that for all sufficiently large \(k\) we obtain \(|e_{n_{k}}^{*}(y)|>\varepsilon/4\). This is impossible, because the coefficients of \(y\) with respect to the Schauder basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) must tend to zero. This contradiction completes the proof. ∎

As an immediate consequence, we obtain the following.

(Strong forward reduction).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon X\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{n\in M}\|T_{n}\|<\varepsilon.\)

We now obtain the following.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i>j\end{subarray}}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

We argue by recursively applying Corollary 3.2 to the columns of \(T\). Choose \(m_{1}=1\). Applying Corollary 3.2 to the \(m_{1}\)th column of \(T\), i.e. to \(TJ_{m_{1}}\), we obtain an infinite subset \(M_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in M_{1}\\ i>m_{1}\end{subarray}}\|T_{i,m_{1}}\|<\varepsilon/2.\)

Suppose now that we have constructed \(1=m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}\) and infinite sets

\(\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq\dots\supseteq M_{k}\)

such that \(m_{j}\in M_{j-1}\) and

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in M_{j}\\ i>m_{j}\end{subarray}}\|T_{i,m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j}\)

for each \(j\leq k\). Choose any \(m_{k+1}\in M_{k}\) with \(m_{k+1}>m_{k}\). Applying Corollary 3.2 to the \(m_{k+1}\)th column of \(T\), restricted to the rows indexed by \(M_{k}\), we obtain an infinite set \(M_{k+1}\subseteq M_{k}\) such that

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in M_{k+1}\\ i>m_{k+1}\end{subarray}}\|T_{i,m_{k+1}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{k+1}.\)

This completes the inductive construction. Set

\(M=\{m_{k}:k\in\mathbb{N}\}.\)

Since \(M\setminus\{m_{1},\dots,m_{j}\}\subseteq M_{j}\) for each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), it follows that

\(\sum_{i>j}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in M_{j}\\ i>m_{j}\end{subarray}}\|T_{i,m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j}\)

for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\). This proves the result. ∎

If one assumes instead that every operator \(S\colon E\to X\) is compact, then one obtains a similar result, namely, a reduction to lower triangular form, by following the ideas developed by Laustsen in . Since this will not be needed for our purposes, we do not make this explicit here.

We now get the claimed upper triangular form.

(Reduction to upper-triangular operators).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-U\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(U\colon E(M,X)\to E(M,X)\) is the upper triangular operator defined by

\(U_{m_{i},m_{j}}=\begin{cases}T_{m_{i},m_{j}},&\text{if }i\leq j,\\ 0,&\text{if }i>j.\end{cases}\)
Proof.Fold proof

By Lemma 3.3, we may choose an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{i>j}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

Define \(U\colon E(M,X)\to E(M,X)\) as in the statement. It is clear that \(U\) defines a linear map, although it need not, a priori, be bounded. The proof that \(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-U\|<\varepsilon\) shows in particular that \(U\) is bounded, with norm at most \(\|T\|+\varepsilon\) and hence an operator.

Let \(x=(x_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\in E(M,X)\) with \(\|x\|\leq 1\). In particular, by \(1\)-unconditionality, we have \(\|x_{m_{j}}\|\leq 1\) for all \(j\in\mathbb{N}\). It follows that

\(\|((P_{M}TJ_{M}-U)x)_{m_{i}}\|\leq\sum_{j<i}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|\|x_{m_{j}}\|\leq\sum_{j<i}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|,\)

and hence, again by \(1\)-unconditionality,

\(\|(P_{M}TJ_{M}-U)x\|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j<i}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i>j}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|<\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon/2^{j}=\varepsilon,\)

where the equality follows by re-indexing the non-negative double series. Therefore, \(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-U\|<\varepsilon\). ∎

Finally, we note that these results apply to \(\ell_{p}\)-sums of \(C(\alpha)\) spaces whenever \(1\leq p<\infty\). The following is well known; we include a proof for completeness.

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal and let \(1\leq p<\infty\). Then every operator \(S\colon C(\alpha)\to\ell_{p}\) is compact.

Proof.Fold proof

By a classical theorem of Pełczyński , every operator from a \(C(K)\)-space into a Banach space either fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\) or is weakly compact. Since \(C(\alpha)^{*}=\ell_{1}(\alpha)\) and \(\ell_{1}(\alpha)\) has the Schur property, every weakly compact operator from \(C(\alpha)\) is compact. It follows that every operator \(S\colon C(\alpha)\to\ell_{p}\) either fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\) or is compact. By Pitt’s theorem, every operator from \(c_{0}\) to \(\ell_{p}\) is compact, and thus no operator \(S\colon C(\alpha)\to\ell_{p}\) can fix a copy of \(c_{0}\). Consequently, every operator from \(C(\alpha)\) to \(\ell_{p}\) is compact. ∎

It is worth noting that these arguments also apply to \(\ell_{p}\)-sums of \(C[0,1]\) for \(1\leq p<2\).

Let \(1\leq p<2\). Then every operator \(S\colon C[0,1]\to\ell_{p}\) is compact.

Proof.Fold proof

This is a standard consequence of classical factorisation theorems. Indeed, \(C[0,1]^{*}\) is an \(L_{1}\)-space, and hence has cotype \(2\). Moreover, \(\ell_{p}\) has cotype \(2\) for \(1\leq p\leq 2\), while \(C[0,1]\) has the approximation property. Therefore, by Pisier’s abstract Grothendieck theorem, see for instance , every operator from \(C[0,1]\) to \(\ell_{p}\) factors through a Hilbert space. Since every operator from a Hilbert space into \(\ell_{p}\), \(1\leq p<2\), is compact by Pitt’s theorem, the result follows. ∎

The previous proposition cannot be extended to \(p\geq 2\), since in that range there are non-compact operators from \(C[0,1]\) to \(\ell_{p}\).

3.1.2.

The \(C[0,1]\) case.

−

We now explain how to obtain the upper triangular reduction in this setting. The key additional ingredient is the isomorphism \(c_{0}(C[0,1])\simeq C[0,1]\), which provides additional room for the gliding-hump argument along \(c_{0}\). Readers familiar with the proof of primariness of \(L_{p}\) by Alspach, Enflo and Odell may recognise a related device: there, the isomorphism \(L_{p}\simeq\ell_{2}(L_{p})\), together with additional properties of the Haar basis, is used to create room along auxiliary \(\ell_{2}\)-coordinates.

(Forward reduction).

Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces and let \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to\ell_{p}(Y)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\|P_{M}TJ_{n}\|<\varepsilon\).

Proof.Fold proof

We proceed by contradiction and assume that the statement is false. Then there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and every infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we have \(\|P_{M}TJ_{n}\|\geq 2\varepsilon\). Choose \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(r\varepsilon^{p}>\|T\|^{p}\), and partition \(\mathbb{N}\) into infinite pairwise disjoint sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{r}\).

By assumption, for each \(s=1,\dots,r\) we have \(\|P_{M_{s}}TJ_{s}\|\geq 2\varepsilon\). Hence, we may choose \(x_{s}\in B_{X}\) and \(x^{*}_{s}\in B_{\ell_{p}(M_{s},Y)^{*}}\) such that \(|x^{*}_{s}P_{M_{s}}TJ_{s}x_{s}|>\varepsilon\).

For each choice of signs \(\theta=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{r})\in\{-1,1\}^{r}\), set

\(x_{\theta}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}\theta_{s}J_{s}x_{s}.\)

Since the vectors \(J_{s}x_{s}\) have disjoint supports in \(c_{0}(X)\), we have \(\|x_{\theta}\|\leq 1\). Thus \(\|Tx_{\theta}\|^{p}\leq\|T\|^{p}\) for every choice of signs, and averaging gives

\(\|T\|^{p}\geq\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|^{p}].\)

Since the sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{r}\) form a partition of \(\mathbb{N}\), we have

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|^{p}]=\sum_{s=1}^{r}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}\|^{p}]\geq\sum_{s=1}^{r}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}|^{p}].\)

For each fixed \(s\), we have

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}|^{p}]=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|\theta_{s}x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}|^{p}]\geq\left|\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}]\right|^{p},\)

where the first equality follows from \(|\theta_{s}|=1\) and the inequality from Jensen’s inequality applied to the convex function \(z\mapsto|z|^{p}\). Moreover,

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}]=\sum_{t=1}^{r}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}\theta_{t}]x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}TJ_{t}x_{t}=x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}TJ_{s}x_{s},\)

because \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}\theta_{t}]=0\) for \(s\neq t\), while \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}^{2}]=1\). Hence

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}Tx_{\theta}|^{p}]\geq|x_{s}^{*}P_{M_{s}}TJ_{s}x_{s}|^{p}>\varepsilon^{p}.\)

Therefore

\(\|T\|^{p}\geq\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|^{p}]>r\varepsilon^{p},\)

contradicting the choice of \(r\). This contradiction proves the result. ∎

Observe that the previous result also applies to \(E\)-sums, that is, to operators \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to E(Y)\), provided that \(E\) has an unconditional basis and no block sequence of the basis of \(E\) spans a copy of \(c_{0}\). Indeed, the same proof applies after splitting \(\mathbb{N}\) into countably many infinite sets \((M_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\); failure of the conclusion would produce, after truncating and passing to a subsequence, a block sequence equivalent to the canonical basis of \(c_{0}\).

We shall use the following notation. For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we denote by

\(\widehat{J}_{n}\colon c_{0}(X)\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\)

the canonical isometric embedding into the \(n\)-th outer coordinate. For each pair \((n,m)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\), we denote by

\(J_{n,m}=\widehat{J}_{n}J_{m}\colon X\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\)

that is, the canonical isometric embedding into the coordinate \((n,m)\), where we recall that \(J_{m}\colon X\to c_{0}(X)\) is the canonical embedding into the \(m\)-th coordinate.

More generally, given two sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), with \(\mathbf{n}\) increasing, we denote by

\(J_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\colon\ell_{p}(X)\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\)

the isometric embedding which places the \(j\)-th coordinate of \(\ell_{p}(X)\) in the coordinate \((n_{j},m_{j})\) of \(\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\). We denote by

\(R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\colon\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\to\ell_{p}(X)\)

the corresponding coordinate projection. Thus, if \(y=(y_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\), then

\(R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}y=(y_{n_{j},m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}.\)

Naturally, \(R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}=I_{\ell_{p}(X)}\). For \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we write \(\widehat{P}_{M}\colon\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\) for the projection onto the outer coordinates belonging to \(M\).

Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), let \(X\) be a Banach space, and let

\(T\colon\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\)

be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and an upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(X)\to\ell_{p}(X)\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-U\|<\varepsilon.\)
Proof.Fold proof

We shall recursively construct pairs \((n_{j},m_{j})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and infinite subsets

\(\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq M_{2}\supseteq\ldots\)

such that, for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(\displaystyle n_{j}\in M_{j-1},\qquad M_{j}\subseteq M_{j-1}\cap\{n\in\mathbb{N}:n>n_{j}\},\)
\(\displaystyle m_{j}>m_{j-1},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\widehat{P}_{M_{j}}TJ_{n_{j},m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1},\)

where we set \(m_{0}=0\).

Suppose that \(M_{j-1}\) has been chosen. Choose \(n_{j}\in M_{j-1}\), and set

\(N_{j}=M_{j-1}\cap\{n\in\mathbb{N}:n>n_{j}\}.\)

Let \(W_{j}\colon c_{0}(X)\to c_{0}(X)\) be the isometric embedding which places the \(k\)-th coordinate of \(c_{0}(X)\) in the coordinate \(m_{j-1}+k\). Applying Lemma 3.8 to the operator

\(\widehat{P}_{N_{j}}T\widehat{J}_{n_{j}}W_{j}\colon c_{0}(X)\to\ell_{p}(N_{j},c_{0}(X)),\)

we obtain \(k_{j}\in\mathbb{N}\) and an infinite subset \(M_{j}\subseteq N_{j}\) such that

\(\|\widehat{P}_{M_{j}}T\widehat{J}_{n_{j}}W_{j}J_{k_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1}.\)

Set \(m_{j}=m_{j-1}+k_{j}\). Since \(W_{j}J_{k_{j}}=J_{m_{j}}\), we have \(\widehat{J}_{n_{j}}W_{j}J_{k_{j}}=J_{n_{j},m_{j}}\). Hence

\(\|\widehat{P}_{M_{j}}TJ_{n_{j},m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1}.\)

This completes the recursive construction. In particular, both \((n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \((m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) are increasing.

Set \(S=R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\) and write \(S=(S_{i,j})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}\) with respect to the natural decomposition of \(\ell_{p}(X)\). For each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), define \(H_{j}\colon X\to\ell_{p}(X)\) coordinate-wise by

\(P_{i}H_{j}x=\begin{cases}S_{i,j}x,&i>j,\\ 0,&i\leq j.\end{cases}\)

If \(i>j\), then \(n_{i}\in M_{j}\). Hence, for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\) and every \(x\in X\), we have

\(\|H_{j}x\|_{\ell_{p}(X)}=\left(\sum_{i>j}\|S_{i,j}x\|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\leq\|\widehat{P}_{M_{j}}TJ_{n_{j},m_{j}}x\|<(\varepsilon/2^{j+1})\|x\|.\)

In particular, \(\|H_{j}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{j+1}\). Define \(L\colon\ell_{p}(X)\to\ell_{p}(X)\) coordinate-wise by

\(P_{i}Lx=\sum_{j<i}S_{i,j}x_{j}\qquad(x=(x_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{p}(X),\ i\in\mathbb{N}).\)

For \(x=(x_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{p}(X)\), we have

\(Lx=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}H_{j}x_{j}.\)

Hence

\(\|Lx\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|H_{j}x_{j}\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\varepsilon/2^{j+1})\|x_{j}\|\leq\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon/2^{j+1}\right)\|x\|=(\varepsilon/2)\|x\|.\)

Thus \(L\) is bounded and \(\|L\|<\varepsilon\). Now set \(U=S-L\). Since \(L\) is precisely the strictly lower triangular part of \(S\), the operator \(U\) is upper triangular. Moreover,

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-U\|=\|S-U\|=\|L\|<\varepsilon.\)

∎

3.2.

Reduction to lower triangular form.

−

We next establish a corresponding reduction to lower triangular form. Together with the preceding reduction, this will yield the desired diagonal form. The argument rests on the topological indivisibility, together with the contrast between the inherently \(\ell_{1}\)-type nature of scalar addition and the fact that disjoint vectors in \(\ell_{p}\) cannot combine in an \(\ell_{1}\)-fashion whenever \(1<p\leq\infty\).

We prove a reduction for row operators to essentially disjoint parts, in the spirit of Corollary 3.2 for column operators. We control the norm of the resulting row operator, rather than the sum of the norms of its entries. Recall that, if \(A\) is a closed subset of \([0,\alpha]\) or \([0,1]\), then \(R_{A}\) denotes the corresponding restriction operator.

(Backward reduction).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and let \(1<p\leq\infty\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to C(K)\) be an operator, written as \(T=(T_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Then there exist an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a closed subset \(A\subseteq K\) homeomorphic to \(K\) such that

\(\|R_{A}TJ_{M}\|\leq\varepsilon.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Let \(K\) be either \([0,\alpha]\) or \([0,1]\). We first consider the case \(1<p<\infty\). Choose \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) satisfying \(N^{\frac{p-1}{p}}>\|T\|/\varepsilon\) and partition \(\mathbb{N}\) into infinite disjoint sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{N}\).

For each \(1\leq n\leq N\), define

\(A_{n}=\{a\in K:\sup_{f\in\ell_{p}(M_{n},C(K)),\,\|f\|\leq 1}|Tf(a)|\leq\varepsilon\}.\)

Then each \(A_{n}\) is a closed subset of \(K\). We claim that \(\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}=K\). Indeed, suppose towards a contradiction that there exists \(a\in K\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}\). By definition, for each \(n=1,\dots,N\), we can find \(f_{n}\in\ell_{p}(M_{n},C(K))\) with \(\|f_{n}\|=1\) and \(Tf_{n}(a)>\varepsilon\). Define \(f=\sum_{n=1}^{N}f_{n}\). Since the \(f_{n}\) have pairwise disjoint supports, \(\|f\|=N^{1/p}\). On the other hand,

\(N\varepsilon<\sum_{n=1}^{N}Tf_{n}(a)=Tf(a)\leq\|T\|\|f\|=\|T\|N^{1/p},\)

which contradicts the choice of \(N\). Hence \(\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}=K\).

It remains only to use the appropriate topological indivisibility statement. If \(K=[0,\alpha]\), then Lemma 2.7 gives \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(A_{n_{0}}\) is homeomorphic to \([0,\alpha]\). Taking \(M=M_{n_{0}}\) and \(A=A_{n_{0}}\) gives the desired conclusion. If \(K=[0,1]\), then Lemma 2.11 gives \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) and a closed subset \(A\subseteq A_{n_{0}}\) homeomorphic to \([0,1]\). Taking \(M=M_{n_{0}}\) gives the desired conclusion, since the defining estimate for \(A_{n_{0}}\) is inherited by closed subsets.

The case \(p=\infty\) is entirely analogous. One chooses \(N>\|T\|/\varepsilon\) instead, and observes that, for \(f=\sum_{n=1}^{N}f_{n}\) with the \(f_{n}\) supported on pairwise disjoint sets \(M_{n}\), we have \(\|f\|=1\). The same contradiction argument gives \(\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}=K\), and the same topological argument finishes the proof. ∎

One can, in fact, obtain a stronger version of the preceding lemma. Indeed, if, in the proof, one partitions \(\mathbb{N}\) into countably many pairwise disjoint subsets \((M_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\), then the same ideas show that the conclusion remains valid for the \(E\)-sum of \(C(\alpha)\), provided that \(E\) is a Banach space with an unconditional basis which does not contain the spaces \(\ell_{1}^{n}\) uniformly as block subspaces. In the case of \(C[0,1]\), using the countable topological indivisibility of \([0,1]\), one obtains the corresponding conclusion under the weaker assumption that no block sequence of the basis of \(E\) spans a copy of \(\ell_{1}\).

The previous lemma is obviously false for \(\ell_{1}\)-sums. Indeed, for example, the operator

\(T\colon\ell_{1}(C(\alpha))\to C(\alpha),\qquad(f_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mapsto\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}f_{n}\)

clearly cannot satisfy the conclusion of the lemma above. Thus, a different argument will be needed in order to obtain a lower triangular reduction in the case \(p=1\).

We obtain the following reduction to lower triangular form. We note that, when \(p=\infty\), the lower triangular operator associated with a given operator is well defined, has norm no greater than that of the original operator, and is lower triangular in the sense of Definition 2.4. By contrast, when \(1<p<\infty\), the lower triangular part is, a priori, only a linear map; its boundedness is established implicitly through the proof of the estimate \(\|RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon\).

(Reduction to lower triangular operators).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and let \(1<p\leq\infty\). Then, for every operator

\(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K)),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a family \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of closed subsets of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon,\)

where

\(R\colon\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{p}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(R=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}:j\in\mathbb{N}),\)

and

\(L\colon\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{p}}\)

is the lower triangular operator defined by

\(L_{m_{i},m_{j}}=\begin{cases}R_{A_{m_{i}}}T_{m_{i},m_{j}},&\text{if }i\geq j,\\ 0,&\text{if }i<j.\end{cases}\)
Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) be fixed. We apply Lemma 3.11 recursively to the rows of \(T\). Choose \(m_{1}=1\). Applying Lemma 3.11 to the operator

\(P_{m_{1}}T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to C(K),\)

we obtain an infinite subset \(M_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a closed subset \(A_{m_{1}}\subseteq K\), homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{1}}}P_{m_{1}}TJ_{M_{1}}\|<\varepsilon/4.\)

Suppose now that we have constructed

\(1=m_{1}<\dots<m_{k},\qquad\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq\dots\supseteq M_{k},\)

and closed sets \(A_{m_{1}},\dots,A_{m_{k}}\subseteq K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that \(m_{j}\in M_{j-1}\) and

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}P_{m_{j}}TJ_{M_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1}\)

for each \(j\leq k\).

Choose any \(m_{k+1}\in M_{k}\) with \(m_{k+1}>m_{k}\). Identifying \(\ell_{p}(M_{k},C(K))\) canonically with \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\), we may apply Lemma 3.11 to

\(P_{m_{k+1}}TJ_{M_{k}}\colon\ell_{p}(M_{k},C(K))\to C(K).\)

We thus obtain an infinite subset \(M_{k+1}\subseteq M_{k}\) and a closed subset \(A_{m_{k+1}}\subseteq K\), homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{k+1}}}P_{m_{k+1}}TJ_{M_{k+1}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{k+2}.\)

This completes the inductive construction.

Set \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\), and define \(R\) and \(L\) as in the statement. It is straightforward to verify that \(L\) is a linear map; its boundedness will follow from the estimates below. Let \(W=RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\). For each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), let

\(Q_{m_{j}}\colon\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{i}})\right)_{\ell_{p}}\to C(A_{m_{j}})\)

denote the coordinate projection onto the \(m_{j}\)-th coordinate. Then, by the definition of \(L\), for every \(x\in\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\) we have

\(Q_{m_{j}}Wx=R_{A_{m_{j}}}P_{m_{j}}TJ_{M}P_{M\setminus\{m_{1},\dots,m_{j}\}}x,\)

where \(P_{M\setminus\{m_{1},\dots,m_{j}\}}\) denotes the coordinate projection on \(\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\) onto the tail coordinates. Since \(M\setminus\{m_{1},\dots,m_{j}\}\subseteq M_{j}\), it follows that

\(\|Q_{m_{j}}W\|\leq\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}P_{m_{j}}TJ_{M_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1}\)

for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\). Finally, let \(x\in\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\) with \(\|x\|\leq 1\). Then

\(\displaystyle\|Wx\|\) \(\displaystyle=\left\|\bigl(Q_{m_{j}}Wx\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\right\|_{\ell_{p}}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|Q_{m_{j}}Wx\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\|Q_{m_{j}}W\|\|x\|\)
\(\displaystyle<\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon/2^{j+1}=\varepsilon/2.\)

Hence \(\|RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|=\|W\|<\varepsilon\). Since \(RP_{M}TJ_{M}\) and \(W\) are bounded, \(L=RP_{M}TJ_{M}-W\) is bounded as well. ∎

In the previous proposition, when we refer to a lower triangular operator in the case \(p=\infty\), we mean this in the sense developed in Section 2. That is, it is not enough for the operator merely to have a lower triangular operator matrix; it must also genuinely act according to that matrix.

3.3.

Dichotomy for upper triangular operators.

−

Finally, the coup de grâce: we show that, if the operator \(T\) is upper triangular, then either \(T\) or \(I-T\) factors the identity on the space. For convenience, we restrict ourselves to the case \(1<p<\infty\). We shall deal with the cases \(p=1\) and \(p=\infty\) later.

(Dichotomy for upper triangular operators).

Let \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Suppose that \(C(K)\) has the \(C\)-PFP, for some constant \(C\geq 1\). Then, for every upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K))\), either \(U\) or \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-U\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) with constant \(2C\).

Proof.Fold proof

Fix an upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K))\) and choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(C\delta<1\) and

\(\frac{C}{1-C\delta}<2C.\)

Applying Proposition 3.13, we obtain an infinite subset

\(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\)

and closed sets \(A_{m_{j}}\subseteq K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|RP_{M}UJ_{M}-L\|<\delta,\)

where \(L\) is lower triangular. Since \(U\) is upper triangular, \(L\) is in fact diagonal.

For each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(V_{j}\colon C(K)\to C(A_{m_{j}})\) be the isometric isomorphism induced by a homeomorphism between \(A_{m_{j}}\) and \(K\), and let \(S_{j}\colon C(A_{m_{j}})\to C(K)\) be a norm-one extension operator, so that

\(R_{A_{m_{j}}}S_{j}=I_{C(A_{m_{j}})}.\)

Define

\(V=\operatorname{diag}(V_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N})\qquad\text{and}\qquad S=\operatorname{diag}(S_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Consider the operator

\(W=V^{-1}RP_{M}UJ_{M}SV\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K)).\)

Since \(\|S\|=\|V\|=\|V^{-1}\|=1\), it follows that

\(\|W-D\|<\delta,\)

where

\(D=V^{-1}LSV.\)

Because \(L\) is diagonal, so is \(D\), say

\(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}),\)

where

\(D_{j}=V_{j}^{-1}R_{A_{m_{j}}}U_{m_{j},m_{j}}S_{j}V_{j}\colon C(K)\to C(K).\)

Since \(C(K)\) has the \(C\)-PFP, for each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\) either \(D_{j}\) or \(I_{C(K)}-D_{j}\) factors \(I_{C(K)}\) with factorisation constant at most \(C\). After passing to a further infinite subset of \(M\) and relabelling, we may suppose that the same alternative holds for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\).

First, suppose that, for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), there exist operators \(\Phi_{j},\Psi_{j}\colon C(K)\to C(K)\) such that

\(\Phi_{j}D_{j}\Psi_{j}=I_{C(K)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi_{j}\|\|\Psi_{j}\|\leq C.\)

Rescaling if necessary, we may assume that

\(\|\Phi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{C}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Psi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{C}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

Define

\(\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Psi=\operatorname{diag}(\Psi_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Then

\(\Phi D\Psi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi\|\|\Psi\|\leq C,\)

hence

\(\Phi W\Psi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}+E,\qquad\text{where}\qquad E=\Phi(W-D)\Psi.\)

Since

\(\|E\|\leq\|\Phi\|\|W-D\|\|\Psi\|\leq C\delta<1,\)

it follows that \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}+E\) is invertible, and

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}=(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}+E)^{-1}\Phi W\Psi.\)

Thus \(W\) factors the identity with factorisation constant at most

\(\frac{C}{1-C\delta}<2C.\)

Since

\(W=V^{-1}RP_{M}UJ_{M}SV,\)

it follows that \(W\) factors through \(U\) with constant one. Hence \(U\) factors the identity with the same bound.

The case where, for every \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), the operator \(I_{C(K)}-D_{j}\) factors \(I_{C(K)}\) is identical. Indeed, in that case, we obtain diagonal operators \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) with

\(\Phi(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-D)\Psi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi\|\|\Psi\|\leq C.\)

Since

\(\|(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-W)-(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-D)\|=\|W-D\|<\delta,\)

the same perturbation argument shows that \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-W\) factors the identity with factorisation constant at most

\(\frac{C}{1-C\delta}<2C.\)

Since

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-W=V^{-1}RP_{M}(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-U)J_{M}SV,\)

it follows that \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-W\) factors through \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-U\) with constant one. Hence \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-U\) factors the identity with the same bound. This completes the proof. ∎

4.

Lower triangular reduction for \(\ell_{1}\)-sums

−

As observed above, Lemma 3.11 fails when \(p=1\), and therefore the lower triangular reduction used in the previous section cannot be applied in this case. We replace it with a different reduction, which uses the special geometry of the outer \(\ell_{1}\)-sum together with the extra room provided by an isomorphism \(E(X)\simeq X\), where \(E\) is either \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{p}\) for some \(1<p<\infty\). The argument is similar in spirit to the use of the \(c_{0}\)-coordinate structure in Section 3.1.2.

Since this can be done in this more abstract setting without any additional work, and since the method may be useful elsewhere, we present the general form below. We begin with an abstract backward reduction, which is the key ingredient in the reduction to lower triangular form.

(Backward reduction).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\varepsilon>0\), and let \(E\) be either \(c_{0}\), \(\ell_{\infty}\), or \(\ell_{p}\) for some \(1<p<\infty\). Let \(T\colon E(X)\to\ell_{1}^{N}(X)\) be an operator. Suppose that \(N\varepsilon>\|T\|\) if \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), and that \(N^{(p-1)/p}\varepsilon>\|T\|\) if \(E=\ell_{p}\) with \(1<p<\infty\). Then there exist \(1\leq n\leq N\) and an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{n}TJ_{M}\|\leq\varepsilon.\)
Proof.Fold proof

We prove the case \(c_{0}(X)\) first. We proceed by contradiction and assume that the statement is false. Thus, for every \(1\leq s\leq N\) and every infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we have \(\|P_{s}TJ_{M}\|>\varepsilon\). Let \(M_{1},\ldots,M_{N}\) be pairwise disjoint infinite subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\).

By assumption, for each \(s=1,\ldots,N\) we have \(\|P_{s}TJ_{M_{s}}\|>\varepsilon\). Hence we may choose \(x_{s}\in B_{c_{0}(M_{s},X)}\) and \(x_{s}^{*}\in B_{X^{*}}\) such that

\(|x_{s}^{*}P_{s}TJ_{M_{s}}x_{s}|>\varepsilon.\)

For each choice of signs \(\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{N})\in\{-1,1\}^{N}\), set

\(x_{\theta}=\sum_{s=1}^{N}\theta_{s}J_{M_{s}}x_{s}.\)

Since the sets \(M_{1},\ldots,M_{N}\) are pairwise disjoint, we have \(\|x_{\theta}\|_{c_{0}(X)}\leq 1\). Thus \(\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}\leq\|T\|\) for every choice of signs, and averaging gives

\(\|T\|\geq\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}].\)

Since the norm on \(\ell_{1}^{N}(X)\) is given by summing the coordinate norms, we have

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}]=\sum_{s=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|P_{s}Tx_{\theta}\|]\geq\sum_{s=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{s}Tx_{\theta}|].\)

For each fixed \(s\), since \(|\theta_{s}|=1\), Jensen’s inequality gives

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{s}Tx_{\theta}|]\geq\left|\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}x_{s}^{*}P_{s}Tx_{\theta}]\right|.\)

Moreover,

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}x_{s}^{*}P_{s}Tx_{\theta}]=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}\theta_{r}]x_{s}^{*}P_{s}TJ_{M_{r}}x_{r}=x_{s}^{*}P_{s}TJ_{M_{s}}x_{s},\)

because \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}\theta_{r}]=0\) for \(s\neq r\), while \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\theta_{s}^{2}]=1\). Hence

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[|x_{s}^{*}P_{s}Tx_{\theta}|]\geq|x_{s}^{*}P_{s}TJ_{M_{s}}x_{s}|>\varepsilon.\)

Therefore

\(\|T\|\geq\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}]>N\varepsilon,\)

contradicting the assumption \(N\varepsilon>\|T\|\).

The proof for \(\ell_{p}(X)\), \(1<p<\infty\), is identical, except that now \(x_{s}\in B_{\ell_{p}(M_{s},X)}\) and \(\|x_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{p}(X)}\leq N^{1/p}\). Hence

\(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}]\leq N^{1/p}\|T\|.\)

The same lower estimate gives \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\|Tx_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{1}^{N}(X)}]>N\varepsilon\), contradicting \(N^{(p-1)/p}\varepsilon>\|T\|\). Finally, the case \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) is identical to the case \(c_{0}(X)\), since disjoint supports give \(\|x_{\theta}\|_{\ell_{\infty}(X)}\leq 1\). ∎

Using this version of backward reduction, we can give a reduction to lower triangular operators. Recall that given two sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), with \(\mathbf{n}\) increasing, we use the notation \(J_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\) and \(R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\) in the natural way, whereas \(\widehat{J}_{n}:c_{0}(X)\to\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) denotes the canonical inclusion into the outer \(n\)-th coordinate, as introduced in Section 3.1.2.

(Reduction to lower triangular form on \(\ell_{1}(E(X))\)).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(E\) be either \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{p}\), where \(1<p\leq\infty\). Let

\(T\colon\ell_{1}(E(X))\to\ell_{1}(E(X))\)

be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and a lower triangular operator \(L\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-L\|<\varepsilon.\)
Proof.Fold proof

We prove the case \(E=c_{0}\); the case \(E=\ell_{p}\), \(1<p\leq\infty\), follows by the same argument, using the second part of Lemma 4.1. Let \(T\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) be fixed. For each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), choose \(N_{k}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(N_{k}\varepsilon/2^{k+1}>\|T\|.\)

We use the following convention. If \(M\subseteq M^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) are infinite, then \(J_{M}\colon c_{0}(M,X)\to c_{0}(X)\) denotes the canonical inclusion, while \(J_{M}^{M^{\prime}}\colon c_{0}(M,X)\to c_{0}(M^{\prime},X)\) denotes the canonical inclusion into \(c_{0}(M^{\prime},X)\).

We recursively construct increasing sequences \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \((m_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\), infinite subsets

\(\mathbb{N}=A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq A_{2}\supseteq\ldots,\)

and, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and each \(j\in A_{k}\), infinite subsets \(M_{j}^{k}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), such that, for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(n_{k}\in A_{k-1},\qquad A_{k}\subseteq A_{k-1}\cap\{j\in\mathbb{N}:j>n_{k}\},\qquad m_{k}>m_{k-1},\)

where \(m_{0}=0\), and

\(\|R_{n_{i},m_{i}}T\widehat{J}_{j}J_{M_{j}^{k}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{i+1}\qquad(1\leq i\leq k,\ j\in A_{k}).\)

Suppose that the construction has been carried out up to stage \(k-1\). Choose distinct elements \(a_{1}<\ldots<a_{N_{k}}\) of \(A_{k-1}\). If \(k=1\), set \(M_{j}^{0}=\mathbb{N}\) for every \(j\in A_{0}\). For each \(1\leq s\leq N_{k}\), choose

\(b_{s}\in M_{a_{s}}^{k-1}\qquad\text{with}\qquad b_{s}>m_{k-1}.\)

Put

\(B=\{j\in A_{k-1}:j>a_{N_{k}}\}.\)

For each \(j\in B\), define \(T_{j}\colon c_{0}(M_{j}^{k-1},X)\to\ell_{1}^{N_{k}}(X)\) by

\(T_{j}x=\bigl(R_{a_{s},b_{s}}T\widehat{J}_{j}J_{M_{j}^{k-1}}x\bigr)_{s=1}^{N_{k}}.\)

We have \(\|T_{j}\|\leq\|T\|\). Hence, by Lemma 4.1, applied after identifying \(c_{0}(M_{j}^{k-1},X)\) with \(c_{0}(X)\), there exist \(1\leq s(j)\leq N_{k}\) and an infinite subset \(L_{j}\subseteq M_{j}^{k-1}\) such that

\(\|R_{a_{s(j)},b_{s(j)}}T\widehat{J}_{j}J_{M_{j}^{k-1}}J_{L_{j}}^{M_{j}^{k-1}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{k+1}.\)

Since \(J_{M_{j}^{k-1}}J_{L_{j}}^{M_{j}^{k-1}}=J_{L_{j}}\), this is

\(\|R_{a_{s(j)},b_{s(j)}}T\widehat{J}_{j}J_{L_{j}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{k+1}.\)

By the pigeonhole principle, we can find \(1\leq s_{k}\leq N_{k}\) and an infinite subset \(A_{k}\subseteq B\) such that \(s(j)=s_{k}\) for every \(j\in A_{k}\). Define

\(n_{k}=a_{s_{k}},\qquad m_{k}=b_{s_{k}}.\)

For \(j\in A_{k}\), define \(M_{j}^{k}=L_{j}\). Since \(M_{j}^{k}\subseteq M_{j}^{k-1}\), all estimates obtained at earlier stages are preserved. The estimate for the new row follows from the choice of \(A_{k}\). This completes the recursive construction.

Define \(S:\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\) by

\(S=R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}.\)

Write \(S=(S_{i,j})_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}\) with respect to the natural decomposition of \(\ell_{1}(X)\). For each \(i,j\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(i<j\), then \(n_{j}\in A_{i}\) and \(m_{j}\in M_{n_{j}}^{i}\). Hence

\(\|S_{i,j}\|=\|R_{n_{i},m_{i}}TJ_{n_{j},m_{j}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{i+1}.\)

Define \(H\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\), the upper triangular part of \(S\), by

\(P_{i}Hx=\sum_{j>i}S_{i,j}x_{j}\qquad(x=(x_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{1}(X)).\)

Then, for every \(x\in\ell_{1}(X)\), we have

\(\|Hx\|_{\ell_{1}(X)}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j>i}\varepsilon/2^{i+1}\|x_{j}\|\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon/2^{i+1}\right)\|x\|_{\ell_{1}(X)}=(\varepsilon/2)\|x\|_{\ell_{1}(X)}.\)

Thus \(\|H\|<\varepsilon\). Therefore, if we let \(L=S-H\), then \(L\) is lower triangular and

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-L\|=\|H\|<\varepsilon.\)

In the case \(E=\ell_{p}\), \(1<p\leq\infty\), the same proof applies with \(c_{0}(M,X)\) replaced by \(\ell_{p}(M,X)\) throughout, and with \(N_{k}\) chosen so that

\(N_{k}^{(p-1)/p}\varepsilon/2^{k+1}>\|T\|\)

in the cases \(1<p<\infty\). ∎

5.

Technical results for \(\ell_{\infty}\)-sums

−

In the previous sections, we exploited the fact that the operator matrix of \(T\colon\allowbreak\ell_{p}(C(K))\allowbreak\to\ell_{p}(C(K))\) encodes all the relevant information about \(T\), whenever \(1\leq p<\infty\). Even though this is no longer true when \(p=\infty\), we will show that this operator matrix is enough for our purposes. Before stating the reduction to diagonal operators, we record the following lemma, which is the counterpart to Lemma 3.1 for the setting \(p=\infty\).

(Forward reduction).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) be an operator with operator matrix \(T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and closed subsets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},n_{0}}\|\leq\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) be fixed. Choose \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) so that \(N>\|T\|/\varepsilon\). For each \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\) define

\(B(n,m)=\{a\in K:\sup_{f\in B_{C(K)}}|T_{m,n}f(a)|\leq\varepsilon\},\)

which is a closed subset of \(K\). Let

\(M_{n}=\{m\in\mathbb{N}:B(n,m)\text{ contains a closed subset homeomorphic to }K\}.\)

We claim that there exists \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(M_{n_{0}}\) is infinite. Indeed, suppose by contradiction that \(M_{n}\) is finite for \(n=1,\ldots,N\). Then we can find

\(m_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}M_{n}.\)

By definition, none of the closed sets \(B(n,m_{0})\) contains a closed subset homeomorphic to \(K\). Hence, by Lemma 2.7 in the ordinal case, and by Lemma 2.11 in the case \(K=[0,1]\), we must have

\(\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}B(n,m_{0})\subsetneq K.\)

Choose \(a\in K\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}B(n,m_{0})\). By definition, for each \(n=1,\ldots,N\) we can find a norm-one function \(f_{n}\in C(K)\) such that \(T_{m_{0},n}f_{n}(a)>\varepsilon\). Let \(f=\sum_{n=1}^{N}J_{n}f_{n}\), so that \(\|f\|=1\) since \(J_{1}f_{1},\ldots,J_{N}f_{N}\) have disjoint supports. It follows that

\(\varepsilon N<\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{m_{0},n}f_{n}(a)=P_{m_{0}}Tf(a)\leq\|Tf\|\leq\|T\|\|f\|=\|T\|,\)

which contradicts our choice of \(N\). This proves the claim.

Choose \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(M_{n_{0}}\) is infinite, and write \(M_{n_{0}}=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\). For each \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), choose a closed subset \(A_{m_{j}}\subseteq B(n_{0},m_{j})\) homeomorphic to \(K\). Since \(A_{m_{j}}\subseteq B(n_{0},m_{j})\), we have

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},n_{0}}\|\leq\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

This completes the proof. ∎

The proof of Lemma 5.1 remains valid for operators

\(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}},\)

provided that each \(A_{m}\) is homeomorphic to \(K\). In that case, one obtains an infinite set \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\) and closed subsets \(B_{m_{j}}\subseteq A_{m_{j}}\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that the corresponding restricted coordinate operators are small.

Using the previous lemma and remark, together with a standard inductive construction, we obtain the following.

(Weak upper triangular reduction).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) be an operator with operator matrix \(T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a strictly increasing sequence \((m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\) and closed subsets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},m_{i}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{i}\qquad\text{for all }i<j.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), set \(A_{n}^{0}=K\).

We construct recursively a strictly increasing sequence \(m_{1}<m_{2}<\ldots\), nested infinite sets

\(\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq M_{2}\supseteq\ldots,\)

and, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and each \(n\in M_{k}\), a closed subset \(A_{n}^{k}\) of \(K\), homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(m_{k}\in M_{k-1},\qquad m_{k}<m_{k+1},\)
\(A_{n}^{k}\subseteq A_{n}^{k-1}\qquad\text{for all }k\in\mathbb{N}\text{ and all }n\in M_{k},\)

and

\(\|R_{A_{n}^{k}}T_{n,m_{k}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{k}\qquad\text{for all }k\in\mathbb{N}\text{ and all }n\in M_{k}.\)

To begin, apply Lemma 5.1 to \(T\) with \(\varepsilon/2\). We obtain \(m_{1}\in\mathbb{N}\), an infinite set \(M_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and, for each \(n\in M_{1}\), a closed subset \(A_{n}^{1}\) of \(K\), homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{n}^{1}}T_{n,m_{1}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2\qquad\text{for all }n\in M_{1}.\)

Suppose now that, for some \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), we have already constructed \(m_{1}<\ldots<m_{k}\), infinite sets

\(\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq\ldots\supseteq M_{k},\)

and closed sets \(A_{n}^{i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\) and \(n\in M_{i}\), satisfying the above conditions.

Since \(M_{k}\) is infinite, the set

\(M_{k}^{\prime}=M_{k}\cap\{n\in\mathbb{N}:n>m_{k}\}\)

is infinite. Identify \(M_{k}^{\prime}\) with \(\mathbb{N}\) via the increasing enumeration, and apply Lemma 5.1 to the corresponding compression of \(T\) to \(M_{k}^{\prime}\). By Remark 5.2, we may do so with the range at coordinate \(n\in M_{k}^{\prime}\) restricted to \(A_{n}^{k}\). We obtain \(m_{k+1}\in M_{k}^{\prime}\), an infinite set \(M_{k+1}\subseteq M_{k}^{\prime}\), and, for each \(n\in M_{k+1}\), a closed subset \(A_{n}^{k+1}\) of \(A_{n}^{k}\), homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{n}^{k+1}}T_{n,m_{k+1}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{k+1}\qquad\text{for all }n\in M_{k+1}.\)

This completes the recursive construction.

Finally, set

\(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\},\qquad A_{m_{j}}=A_{m_{j}}^{j-1}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

This is well defined because \(m_{j}\in M_{j-1}\).

Let \(1\leq i<j\). Since \(m_{j}\in M_{j-1}\subseteq M_{i}\), the set \(A_{m_{j}}^{i}\) is defined and, by construction, \(A_{m_{j}}=A_{m_{j}}^{j-1}\subseteq A_{m_{j}}^{i}\). It follows that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},m_{i}}\|\leq\|R_{A_{m_{j}}^{i}}T_{m_{j},m_{i}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{i}.\)

This proves the result. ∎

(Lower triangular to diagonal reduction).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\) for some ordinal \(\eta\). Then, for every lower triangular operator

\(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K)),\qquad\text{with operator matrix }L=(L_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a family \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of closed subsets of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|RP_{M}LJ_{M}-D\|\leq\varepsilon,\)

where

\(R\colon\ell_{\infty}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(R=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}:j\in\mathbb{N}),\)

and

\(D\colon\ell_{\infty}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(D=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}L_{m_{j},m_{j}}:j\in\mathbb{N}).\)
Proof.Fold proof

Suppose that \(L\) is lower triangular and let \(\varepsilon>0\) be fixed. By Lemma 5.3, we can find an infinite set \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and closed subsets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{i}}}L_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{j}\qquad\text{for all }j<i.\)

We claim that defining \(R\) and \(D\) as in the statement works. To this end, set

\(W=RP_{M}LJ_{M}-D.\)

Then \(W\) is lower triangular, since \(L\) is lower triangular and \(D\) is diagonal. Moreover, for each \(i\in\mathbb{N}\), let

\(Q_{m_{i}}\colon\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\to C(A_{m_{i}})\)

denote the canonical projection onto the \(i\)-th coordinate. Since \(W\) is lower triangular and \(Q_{m_{i}}WJ_{m_{i}}=0\) for every \(i\in\mathbb{N}\), it follows that, for each fixed \(i\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(\|Q_{m_{i}}W\|\leq\sum_{j<i}\|Q_{m_{i}}WJ_{m_{j}}\|=\sum_{j<i}\|R_{A_{m_{i}}}L_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|\leq\sum_{j<i}\varepsilon/2^{j}<\varepsilon.\)

Therefore,

\(\|W\|=\sup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\|Q_{m_{i}}W\|\leq\varepsilon,\)

which completes the proof. ∎

This reduction also holds in the case \(1<p<\infty\), with an almost identical proof, and one could in fact use it to give a unified treatment of the cases \(1<p\leq\infty\). However, the case \(p=\infty\) is slightly more delicate: one must take care with the identification of an operator and its matrix, and Lemma 5.3 requires an additional projection onto the sets \(A_{m_{j}}\), whereas its counterpart, Lemma 3.3, does not. For the sake of clarity, we have therefore chosen to treat these cases separately.

We can finally state the dichotomy for lower triangular operators.

(Dichotomy for lower triangular operators).

Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and suppose that \(C(K)\) has the \(C\)-PFP for some constant \(C\geq 1\). Then, for every lower triangular operator \(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\), either \(L\) or \(I_{\ell_{\infty}(C(K))}-L\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) with constant \(2C\).

Proof.Fold proof

The proof is identical to that of Proposition 3.15, replacing Proposition 3.13 with Lemma 5.4. Indeed, by Lemma 5.4, every lower triangular operator is, after passing to suitable complemented copies of the space, an arbitrarily small perturbation of a diagonal operator. The same diagonal UPFP argument and perturbation argument therefore yield the conclusion. We omit the details. ∎
