We now turn to the proof of our main results.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.Fold proof

Let \(\alpha\) be any ordinal and note that by Theorem 2.6, we have

\([0,\alpha]\cong[0,\omega^{\eta}\cdot n]\)

for some ordinal \(\eta\) and some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Consequently,

\(\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\simeq\ell_{p}(C(\omega^{\eta}\cdot n))\simeq\ell_{p}(C(\omega^{\eta})),\)

so, without loss of generality, we may assume that \(\alpha=\omega^{\eta}\). In particular, \([0,\alpha]\) has characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Let such an \(\alpha\) be fixed from now on. Further, observe that by Theorem 2.10, the space \(C(\alpha)\) has the UPFP. In particular, it has the \(C\)-PFP for some constant \(C\geq 1\).

We start by considering the case \(1<p<\infty\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\to\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\) be an operator, represented as a matrix \(T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) small enough so that \(2C\varepsilon<1/2\).

By Proposition 3.6, every operator from \(C(\alpha)\) to \(\ell_{p}\) is compact. Hence, by Proposition 3.5, we can find an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(P_{M}TJ_{M}=U+E,\)

where \(U\) is upper triangular and \(\|E\|<\varepsilon\).

By Proposition 3.15, after identifying \(\ell_{p}(M,C(\alpha))\) canonically with \(\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\), there exist operators \(\Psi\) and \(\Phi\) with \(\|\Psi\|\|\Phi\|\leq 2C\) such that either \(\Psi U\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}\) or \(\Psi(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}-U)\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}\).

Suppose first that \(\Psi U\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}\). Then

\(\Psi P_{M}TJ_{M}\Phi=\Psi(U+E)\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi.\)

Since

\(\|\Psi E\Phi\|\leq\|\Psi\|\|E\|\|\Phi\|<2C\varepsilon<1/2,\)

the operator \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi\) is invertible, and

\(\|(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi)^{-1}\|\leq\frac{1}{1-\|\Psi E\Phi\|}<2.\)

Therefore,

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}=(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi)^{-1}\Psi P_{M}TJ_{M}\Phi.\)

Hence

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}=\bigl((I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi)^{-1}\Psi P_{M}\bigr)\,T\,\bigl(J_{M}\Phi\bigr),\)

so \(T\) factors the identity. Moreover, the factorisation constant is bounded by

\(\|(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}+\Psi E\Phi)^{-1}\Psi P_{M}\|\,\|J_{M}\Phi\|\leq 2\|\Psi\|\|\Phi\|\leq 4C.\)

The case where \(\Psi(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}-U)\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}\) is identical. Indeed, in that case, one applies the same perturbation argument to

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}-P_{M}TJ_{M}=P_{M}(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}-T)J_{M},\)

and concludes that \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))}-T\) factors the identity with the same bound.

In the case \(p=\infty\), one first applies Proposition 3.13 to obtain an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), closed sets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) each homeomorphic to \([0,\alpha]\), and a lower triangular operator

\(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(M,C(\alpha))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\)

such that

\(\|RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon.\)

Since each \(A_{m_{j}}\) is homeomorphic to \([0,\alpha]\), after making the canonical identifications we may regard \(L\) as a lower triangular operator on \(\ell_{\infty}(C(\alpha))\). By Proposition 5.6, either \(L\) or \(I_{\ell_{\infty}(C(\alpha))}-L\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{\infty}(C(\alpha))\) with constant \(2C\). The same perturbation argument as above then shows that either \(T\) or \(I_{\ell_{\infty}(C(\alpha))}-T\) factors the identity, with the same type of estimate on the factorisation constant.

Finally, the deduction of primariness from the UPFP is standard, via Pełczyński’s decomposition method and the \(\ell_{p}\)-stability of the spaces involved. ∎

The key ingredients in the proofs are Lemmas 3.1 and 3.11. The former remains valid for \(E\)-sums whenever \(E\) has a \(1\)-unconditional basis and contains no copy of \(c_{0}\), while, by Remark 3.12, the latter remains valid for \(E\)-sums of \(C(\alpha)\) whenever \(E\) has a \(1\)-unconditional basis and does not contain the spaces \(\ell_{1}^{n}\) uniformly as block subspaces. It follows that the UPFP also holds for \(E\)-sums of \(C(\alpha)\) spaces whenever \(E\) has a (sub)symmetric basis and satisfies these additional assumptions.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.Fold proof

Suppose first that \(1<p<\infty\). Since \(c_{0}(C[0,1])\) is isomorphic to \(C[0,1]\), it is enough to prove that \(\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))\) has the UPFP. By Proposition 2.14, the space \(C[0,1]\) has the UPFP. In particular, it has the \(C\)-PFP for some constant \(C\geq 1\).

Let \(T\colon\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))\) be an operator, and choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(2C\varepsilon<1/2\). By Lemma 3.10, there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and an upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\to\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-U\|<\varepsilon.\)

Set

\(E=R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-U.\)

By Proposition 3.15, either \(U\) or \(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}-U\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) with constant \(2C\). Suppose first that \(U\) factors the identity. Then there exist operators \(\Psi,\Phi\colon\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\to\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) such that

\(\Psi U\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Psi\|\|\Phi\|\leq 2C.\)

Hence

\(\Psi R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\Phi=I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}+\Psi E\Phi.\)

Since

\(\|\Psi E\Phi\|\leq\|\Psi\|\|E\|\|\Phi\|<2C\varepsilon<1/2,\)

the operator \(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}+\Psi E\Phi\) is invertible, with inverse of norm at most \(2\). Therefore

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}=(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}+\Psi E\Phi)^{-1}\Psi R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\Phi.\)

Hence \(T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) with factorisation constant at most \(4C\).

The case where \(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}-U\) factors the identity is identical. Indeed, since

\(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}-R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}=R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}(I_{\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))}-T)J_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\)

and

\(\|(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}-R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}})-(I_{\ell_{p}(C[0,1])}-U)\|=\|E\|<\varepsilon,\)

the same perturbation argument shows that \(I_{\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))}-T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) with factorisation constant at most \(4C\). Since \(c_{0}(C[0,1])\) is isomorphic to \(C[0,1]\), this shows that either \(T\) or \(I_{\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))}-T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(c_{0}(C[0,1]))\) with uniform control over the constant, which proves the result.

The case \(p=\infty\) is identical to the proof of Theorem 1.1. Briefly, given an operator \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C[0,1])\to\ell_{\infty}(C[0,1])\), one applies Proposition 3.13 to pass, after restricting to suitable closed copies of \([0,1]\), to a lower triangular operator. Then Proposition 5.6 shows that either this lower triangular operator or its complement factors the identity with uniform constant. The same perturbation argument as above then implies that either \(T\) or \(I_{\ell_{\infty}(C[0,1])}-T\) factors the identity, again with a uniform constant. Hence \(\ell_{\infty}(C[0,1])\) has the UPFP.

Primariness follows again from the UPFP and Pełczyński’s decomposition method, by using the \(\ell_{p}\)-stability of the spaces involved. ∎

The key ingredients in the proofs for the \(C[0,1]\) case are Lemmas 3.8 and 3.11. By Remark 3.9, the former remains valid for \(E\)-sums, that is, for operators \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to E(Y)\), whenever \(E\) contains no copy of \(c_{0}\). On the other hand, by Remark 3.12, the latter remains valid for \(E\)-sums of \(C[0,1]\) whenever \(E\) contains no copy of \(\ell_{1}\). By a classical theorem of James , a Banach space with an unconditional basis is reflexive if and only if it contains neither \(c_{0}\) nor \(\ell_{1}\). In particular, the UPFP also holds for \(E\)-sums of \(C[0,1]\) whenever \(E\) is reflexive and has a subsymmetric basis.

We now give the proof for the case \(p=1\).

Proof of Theorem 1.3.Fold proof

Suppose first that \(X\simeq c_{0}(X)\). Since \(\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}(X)\), it is enough to prove that \(\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) has the UPFP. Let \(C\geq 1\) be such that \(X\) has the \(C\)-PFP, and choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(C\varepsilon<1/2\).

We first note that every operator \(S\colon X\to\ell_{1}\) is compact. Indeed, if some such \(S\) were not compact, then \(S\) would not be weakly compact, since \(\ell_{1}\) has the Schur property. Thus, by a result of Pełczyński , \(S\) would fix a copy of \(\ell_{1}\), which yields a complemented copy of \(\ell_{1}\) in \(X\), contradicting the assumption.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\to\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) be an operator. By Proposition 4.2, there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and a lower triangular operator \(L\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-L\|<\varepsilon/2.\)

Since every operator \(X\to\ell_{1}\) is compact, Proposition 3.5, applied to \(L\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\), gives an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and an upper triangular operator \(D\colon\ell_{1}(M,X)\to\ell_{1}(M,X)\) such that

\(\|P_{M}LJ_{M}-D\|<\varepsilon/2.\)

Since \(L\) is lower triangular, \(D\) is diagonal. Moreover,

\(\|P_{M}R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{M}-D\|\leq\|P_{M}(R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-L)J_{M}\|+\|P_{M}LJ_{M}-D\|<\varepsilon.\)

Write \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_{j}:j\in M)\). Since \(X\) has the \(C\)-PFP, for each \(j\in M\) either \(D_{j}\) or \(I_{X}-D_{j}\) factors \(I_{X}\) with constant at most \(C\). Passing to a further infinite subset of \(M\), and relabelling, we may suppose that the same alternative holds for every \(j\in M\).

Suppose first that each \(D_{j}\) factors \(I_{X}\). Then there are operators \(\Phi_{j},\Psi_{j}\colon X\to X\) such that

\(\Phi_{j}D_{j}\Psi_{j}=I_{X}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi_{j}\|\|\Psi_{j}\|\leq C.\)

Rescaling if necessary, we may assume that \(\|\Phi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{C}\) and \(\|\Psi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{C}\) for every \(j\in M\). Thus the diagonal operators \(\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{j}:j\in M)\) and \(\Psi=\operatorname{diag}(\Psi_{j}:j\in M)\) are bounded on \(\ell_{1}(M,X)\) and satisfy

\(\Phi D\Psi=I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi\|\|\Psi\|\leq C.\)

Set

\(E=P_{M}R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{M}-D.\)

Then \(\|E\|<\varepsilon\), and hence \(\|\Phi E\Psi\|<1/2\). Therefore

\(I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}=(I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}+\Phi E\Psi)^{-1}\Phi P_{M}R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{M}\Psi.\)

Thus \(T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{1}(M,X)\), with constant bounded independently of \(T\).

The case where each \(I_{X}-D_{j}\) factors \(I_{X}\) is identical. Indeed, in that case we obtain diagonal operators \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) such that

\(\Phi(I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}-D)\Psi=I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\Phi\|\|\Psi\|\leq C.\)

Since

\(I_{\ell_{1}(M,X)}-P_{M}R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{M}=P_{M}R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}(I_{\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))}-T)J_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}J_{M},\)

the same perturbation argument shows that \(I_{\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))}-T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{1}(M,X)\), again with a constant bounded independently of \(T\).

Identifying \(\ell_{1}(M,X)\) with \(\ell_{1}(X)\), and using the fixed isomorphism \(\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\simeq\ell_{1}(X)\), we conclude that either \(T\) or \(I_{\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))}-T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) with a uniform constant. Hence \(\ell_{1}(c_{0}(X))\) has the UPFP, and therefore so does \(\ell_{1}(X)\).

If \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1<p<\infty\), the proof is the same, replacing \(c_{0}(X)\) by \(\ell_{p}(X)\) throughout and using the \(\ell_{p}\)-version of Proposition 4.2. Thus \(\ell_{1}(\ell_{p}(X))\) has the UPFP, and since \(\ell_{1}(\ell_{p}(X))\simeq\ell_{1}(X)\), the space \(\ell_{1}(X)\) has the UPFP.

Finally, primariness follows from the UPFP and Pełczyński’s decomposition method. ∎

The reader may notice that similar results remain valid under more general assumptions. For example, one can also obtain the UPFP, and thus primariness, for the spaces

\(\Bigl(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C(\omega^{\omega^{\alpha_{n}}})\Bigr)_{p},\qquad 1\leq p\leq\infty,\)

whenever \((\alpha_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is an increasing sequence of countable ordinals. Further variations of this kind are also possible and follow essentially from the same ideas.

Naturally, the previous theorems can be extended to finite iterated sums of the form \(\ell_{p_{1}}(\ell_{p_{2}}(\ldots(\ell_{p_{n}}(C(K)))\ldots))\). This can be done by combining the techniques of with the ideas developed above. Since we do not currently see any applications of this extension, we do not include the details. Similar considerations will apply to iterated sums of the form in Remark 6.3.

toc.title: Sums of Banach spaces with respect to an unconditional basis.
Background and topological results in \(C(\alpha)\)
Background and topological results in \(C[0,1]\)

results.statementHtml: For every ordinal \(\alpha\) and every \(1<p\leq\infty\), the space \(\ell_{p}(C(\alpha))\) has the UPFP. In particular, these spaces are primary.
For every \(1<p\leq\infty\), the space \(\ell_{p}(C[0,1])\) has the UPFP. In particular, these spaces are primary.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space such that either \(X\simeq c_{0}(X)\) or \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1<p\leq\infty\). Suppose moreover that \(X\) contains no complemented copy of \(\ell_{1}\). Then the UPFP passes from \(X\) to \(\ell_{1}(X)\); that is, if \(X\) has the UPFP, then \(\ell_{1}(X)\) has the UPFP. In particular, \(\ell_{1}(X)\) is primary.
Let \(K\) be a compact metric space and let \(1\leq p\leq\infty\). Then \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) is primary.

Let \(T\colon X\to Y\) and \(S\colon Z\to W\) be operators between Banach spaces \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) and \(W\). We say that \(S\) factors through \(T\) with constant \(C\) if there exist operators \(V\colon Z\to X\) and \(U\colon Y\to W\) such that

\(UTV=S\quad\text{and}\quad\|U\|\|V\|\leq C.\)

If this holds for some constant \(C\geq 1\), then we simply say that \(S\) factors through \(T\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space.

  1. (a)

    We say that \(X\) has the primary factorisation property (PFP) if for every bounded operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(C\geq 1\). We say that \(X\) has the \(C\)-primary factorisation property (\(C\)-PFP) if, for every operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\) with constant \(C\).

  3. (c)

    We say that \(X\) has the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP) if there exists \(C\geq 1\) such that \(X\) has the \(C\)-PFP.

Let \(X=\mathbb{K}\) and consider the operator \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(\mathbb{K})\to\ell_{\infty}(\mathbb{K})\) given by

\(Tx=(\Lambda(x),0,0,\dots),\)

where \(\Lambda\) is a Banach limit; see, for instance, . Thus \(\Lambda\in\ell_{\infty}^{*}\), and \(\Lambda\) agrees with the usual limit on convergent sequences. In particular, \(\Lambda\) vanishes on \(c_{0}\). Hence \(T\neq 0\), while \(T_{n,m}=P_{n}TJ_{m}=0\) for all \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\), since \(J_{m}\mathbb{K}\subseteq c_{0}\).

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator. We say that \(T\) is lower triangular if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n<m,\)

and, moreover, \(T\) acts according to its matrix, in the sense that

\(P_{n}Tx=\sum_{m\leq n}T_{n,m}x_{m}\)

for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\).

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator. We say that \(T\) is diagonal if

\(T_{n,m}=0\qquad\text{whenever }n\neq m,\)

and, moreover, \(T\) acts according to its matrix, in the sense that

\(P_{m}Tx=T_{m,m}x_{m}\)

for all \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\).

For the interval formula below, assume η > 0. If η = 0, A is instead a finite discrete set of n points.

Let \(A\) be a compact subset of an ordinal space with characteristic system \((\eta,n)\), where \(\eta\) is an ordinal and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Then \(A\) is homeomorphic to \([0,\omega^{\eta}\cdot n]\).

Correction in this reading edition

The ordinal interval formula applies to positive Cantor–Bendixson rank. At rank zero, A is a finite discrete set of n points, while [0, n] has n + 1 points. The finite case is stated separately here.

results.title: (Finite indivisibility of closed subsets of ordinal intervals).
results.statementHtml: Let \(A\) be a closed subset of an ordinal space with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\) for some ordinal \(\eta\). Suppose that \(A_{1},\dots,A_{N}\subseteq A\) are closed subsets such that \(A=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}A_{n}\). Then there exists \(1\leq n_{0}\leq N\) such that \(A_{n_{0}}\) is homeomorphic to \(A\).

Let \(K\) be a compact Hausdorff space and let \(A\subseteq K\) be closed. Denote by \(R_{A}\colon C(K)\to C(A)\) the restriction operator. We say that an operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C(K)\) is a simultaneous extension operator if

\(R_{A}S_{A}=I_{C(A)}.\)

results.title: (Simultaneous extension operator).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal, and let \(A\) be a closed subset of \([0,\alpha]\). Then there exists a norm-one simultaneous extension operator

\(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C(\alpha).\)

results.title: (Alspach–Benyamini).
results.statementHtml: Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Suppose that \(C(\alpha)\) is not isomorphic to \(C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular ordinal \(\xi\) and any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq 2\). Then \(C(\alpha)\) has the UPFP.

results.title: (Countable topological indivisibility of \([0,1]\)).
results.statementHtml:
Let \((A_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of closed subsets of \([0,1]\) such that

\([0,1]=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_{n}.\)

Then there exist \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) and a closed subset \(A\subseteq A_{n_{0}}\) such that \(A\) is homeomorphic to \([0,1]\).

results.title: (Borsuk–Dugundji extension theorem).
results.statementHtml:
Assume that A is nonempty.

Let \(A\) be a closed subset of \([0,1]\). Then there exists a norm-one simultaneous extension operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C[0,1]\).

Correction in this reading edition

The norm-one conclusion requires A to be nonempty. For A empty, its function space is zero and the extension has norm zero.

Throughout this paper, \(A\) will be a closed interval, so one does not need the full strength of the Borsuk–Dugundji extension theorem. Indeed, if \(A=[a,b]\subseteq[0,1]\), a norm-one extension operator \(S_{A}\colon C(A)\to C[0,1]\) can be obtained by linear interpolation.
The space \(C[0,1]\) has the UPFP.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon X\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\)

we have

\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\|T_{n}\|=0.\)

results.title: (Strong forward reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon X\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{n\in M}\|T_{n}\|<\varepsilon.\)

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i>j\end{subarray}}\|T_{m_{i},m_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

If one assumes instead that every operator \(S\colon E\to X\) is compact, then one obtains a similar result, namely, a reduction to lower triangular form, by following the ideas developed by Laustsen in . Since this will not be needed for our purposes, we do not make this explicit here.

results.title: (Reduction to upper-triangular operators).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Suppose that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) is compact. Then, for every operator

\(T\colon E(\mathbb{N},X)\to E(\mathbb{N},X),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-U\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(U\colon E(M,X)\to E(M,X)\) is the upper triangular operator defined by

\(U_{m_{i},m_{j}}=\begin{cases}T_{m_{i},m_{j}},&\text{if }i\leq j,\\ 0,&\text{if }i>j.\end{cases}\)
Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal and let \(1\leq p<\infty\). Then every operator \(S\colon C(\alpha)\to\ell_{p}\) is compact.
Let \(1\leq p<2\). Then every operator \(S\colon C[0,1]\to\ell_{p}\) is compact.

results.title: (Forward reduction).
results.statementHtml: Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces and let \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to\ell_{p}(Y)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\|P_{M}TJ_{n}\|<\varepsilon\).

Observe that the previous result also applies to \(E\)-sums, that is, to operators \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to E(Y)\), provided that \(E\) has an unconditional basis and no block sequence of the basis of \(E\) spans a copy of \(c_{0}\). Indeed, the same proof applies after splitting \(\mathbb{N}\) into countably many infinite sets \((M_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{N}}\); failure of the conclusion would produce, after truncating and passing to a subsequence, a block sequence equivalent to the canonical basis of \(c_{0}\).

Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), let \(X\) be a Banach space, and let

\(T\colon\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\to\ell_{p}(c_{0}(X))\)

be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and an upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(X)\to\ell_{p}(X)\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-U\|<\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Backward reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and let \(1<p\leq\infty\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to C(K)\) be an operator, written as \(T=(T_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Then there exist an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a closed subset \(A\subseteq K\) homeomorphic to \(K\) such that

\(\|R_{A}TJ_{M}\|\leq\varepsilon.\)

One can, in fact, obtain a stronger version of the preceding lemma. Indeed, if, in the proof, one partitions \(\mathbb{N}\) into countably many pairwise disjoint subsets \((M_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\), then the same ideas show that the conclusion remains valid for the \(E\)-sum of \(C(\alpha)\), provided that \(E\) is a Banach space with an unconditional basis which does not contain the spaces \(\ell_{1}^{n}\) uniformly as block subspaces. In the case of \(C[0,1]\), using the countable topological indivisibility of \([0,1]\), one obtains the corresponding conclusion under the weaker assumption that no block sequence of the basis of \(E\) spans a copy of \(\ell_{1}\).

results.title: (Reduction to lower triangular operators).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and let \(1<p\leq\infty\). Then, for every operator

\(T\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K)),\qquad T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a family \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of closed subsets of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|RP_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon,\)

where

\(R\colon\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{p}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(R=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}:j\in\mathbb{N}),\)

and

\(L\colon\ell_{p}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{p}}\)

is the lower triangular operator defined by

\(L_{m_{i},m_{j}}=\begin{cases}R_{A_{m_{i}}}T_{m_{i},m_{j}},&\text{if }i\geq j,\\ 0,&\text{if }i<j.\end{cases}\)

In the previous proposition, when we refer to a lower triangular operator in the case \(p=\infty\), we mean this in the sense developed in Section 2. That is, it is not enough for the operator merely to have a lower triangular operator matrix; it must also genuinely act according to that matrix.

results.title: (Dichotomy for upper triangular operators).
results.statementHtml: Let \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Suppose that \(C(K)\) has the \(C\)-PFP, for some constant \(C\geq 1\). Then, for every upper triangular operator \(U\colon\ell_{p}(C(K))\to\ell_{p}(C(K))\), either \(U\) or \(I_{\ell_{p}(C(K))}-U\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{p}(C(K))\) with constant \(2C\).

results.title: (Backward reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\varepsilon>0\), and let \(E\) be either \(c_{0}\), \(\ell_{\infty}\), or \(\ell_{p}\) for some \(1<p<\infty\). Let \(T\colon E(X)\to\ell_{1}^{N}(X)\) be an operator. Suppose that \(N\varepsilon>\|T\|\) if \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), and that \(N^{(p-1)/p}\varepsilon>\|T\|\) if \(E=\ell_{p}\) with \(1<p<\infty\). Then there exist \(1\leq n\leq N\) and an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{n}TJ_{M}\|\leq\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Reduction to lower triangular form on \(\ell_{1}(E(X))\)).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(E\) be either \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{p}\), where \(1<p\leq\infty\). Let

\(T\colon\ell_{1}(E(X))\to\ell_{1}(E(X))\)

be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and a lower triangular operator \(L\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\), such that

\(\|R_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-L\|<\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Forward reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) be an operator with operator matrix \(T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and closed subsets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},n_{0}}\|\leq\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }j\in\mathbb{N}.\)

The proof of Lemma 5.1 remains valid for operators

\(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}},\)

provided that each \(A_{m}\) is homeomorphic to \(K\). In that case, one obtains an infinite set \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\) and closed subsets \(B_{m_{j}}\subseteq A_{m_{j}}\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that the corresponding restricted coordinate operators are small.

results.title: (Weak upper triangular reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) be an operator with operator matrix \(T=(T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a strictly increasing sequence \((m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\mathbb{N}\) and closed subsets \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|R_{A_{m_{j}}}T_{m_{j},m_{i}}\|\leq\varepsilon/2^{i}\qquad\text{for all }i<j.\)

results.title: (Lower triangular to diagonal reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\) for some ordinal \(\eta\). Then, for every lower triangular operator

\(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K)),\qquad\text{with operator matrix }L=(L_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}},\)

and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and a family \((A_{m_{j}})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) of closed subsets of \(K\), each homeomorphic to \(K\), such that

\(\|RP_{M}LJ_{M}-D\|\leq\varepsilon,\)

where

\(R\colon\ell_{\infty}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(R=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}:j\in\mathbb{N}),\)

and

\(D\colon\ell_{\infty}(M,C(K))\to\left(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb{N}}C(A_{m_{j}})\right)_{\ell_{\infty}}\)

is the diagonal operator defined by

\(D=\operatorname{diag}(R_{A_{m_{j}}}L_{m_{j},m_{j}}:j\in\mathbb{N}).\)

This reduction also holds in the case \(1<p<\infty\), with an almost identical proof, and one could in fact use it to give a unified treatment of the cases \(1<p\leq\infty\). However, the case \(p=\infty\) is slightly more delicate: one must take care with the identification of an operator and its matrix, and Lemma 5.3 requires an additional projection onto the sets \(A_{m_{j}}\), whereas its counterpart, Lemma 3.3, does not. For the sake of clarity, we have therefore chosen to treat these cases separately.

results.title: (Dichotomy for lower triangular operators).
results.statementHtml: Let \(K\) be either \([0,1]\) or an ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) with characteristic system \((\eta,1)\), and suppose that \(C(K)\) has the \(C\)-PFP for some constant \(C\geq 1\). Then, for every lower triangular operator \(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\to\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\), either \(L\) or \(I_{\ell_{\infty}(C(K))}-L\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{\infty}(C(K))\) with constant \(2C\).

The key ingredients in the proofs are Lemmas 3.1 and 3.11. The former remains valid for \(E\)-sums whenever \(E\) has a \(1\)-unconditional basis and contains no copy of \(c_{0}\), while, by Remark 3.12, the latter remains valid for \(E\)-sums of \(C(\alpha)\) whenever \(E\) has a \(1\)-unconditional basis and does not contain the spaces \(\ell_{1}^{n}\) uniformly as block subspaces. It follows that the UPFP also holds for \(E\)-sums of \(C(\alpha)\) spaces whenever \(E\) has a (sub)symmetric basis and satisfies these additional assumptions.

The key ingredients in the proofs for the \(C[0,1]\) case are Lemmas 3.8 and 3.11. By Remark 3.9, the former remains valid for \(E\)-sums, that is, for operators \(T\colon c_{0}(X)\to E(Y)\), whenever \(E\) contains no copy of \(c_{0}\). On the other hand, by Remark 3.12, the latter remains valid for \(E\)-sums of \(C[0,1]\) whenever \(E\) contains no copy of \(\ell_{1}\). By a classical theorem of James , a Banach space with an unconditional basis is reflexive if and only if it contains neither \(c_{0}\) nor \(\ell_{1}\). In particular, the UPFP also holds for \(E\)-sums of \(C[0,1]\) whenever \(E\) is reflexive and has a subsymmetric basis.

The reader may notice that similar results remain valid under more general assumptions. For example, one can also obtain the UPFP, and thus primariness, for the spaces

\(\Bigl(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C(\omega^{\omega^{\alpha_{n}}})\Bigr)_{p},\qquad 1\leq p\leq\infty,\)

whenever \((\alpha_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is an increasing sequence of countable ordinals. Further variations of this kind are also possible and follow essentially from the same ideas.

Naturally, the previous theorems can be extended to finite iterated sums of the form \(\ell_{p_{1}}(\ell_{p_{2}}(\ldots(\ell_{p_{n}}(C(K)))\ldots))\). This can be done by combining the techniques of with the ideas developed above. Since we do not currently see any applications of this extension, we do not include the details. Similar considerations will apply to iterated sums of the form in Remark 6.3.

theorem-1-1.note: The formal theorem proves both the UPFP and primariness for every ordinal and every p ≥ 1, including p = ∞.
